title: Blood lead secular trend in a cohort of children in Mexico City (1987-2002).
ehr_evidence: We recruited 502 pregnant women attending the prenatal clinic at 12 weeks of pregnancy at the National Institute of Perinatology in Mexico City and followed 321 children through structured interviews of the parents and with psychometric tests and blood lead determinations every 6 months from delivery; blood samples were analyzed by anodic stripping voltammetry at ESA Labs, and air lead was obtained from the Automatic Network of Atmospheric Monitoring (ANAM) of the Metropolitan Zone of the Valley of Mexico.
summary: A prospective birth cohort of 321 children born in Mexico City between 1987 and 1992, followed every 6 months for 10 years, examined the secular trend in blood lead levels and the relative contribution of air lead, lead-glazed ceramics, socioeconomic status, and place of residence.
key_findings: Yearly mean air lead of the Valley of Mexico decreased from 2.80 µg/m3 in 1987 to 0.07 µg/m3 in 2002.

The contribution of air lead to blood lead was strongest for subjects born in 1987 (each natural log decrease in air lead accompanied by a 23.7% decrease in blood lead) and fell to nearly zero for children born in 1992.

The geometric mean of blood lead rose from 8.4 µg/dL (95% CI, 7.7 to 9.2) in the first year of life to 10.1 µg/dL (95% CI, 9.3 to 11.0) in the second year and decreased to 6.4 µg/dL (95% CI, 5.8 to 7.1) at 10 years of age.
Children of families using lead-glazed ceramics had blood lead levels 18.5% (95% CI, 10.0 to 27.6) higher than children of nonusing families.
Children in the lowest socioeconomic stratum had blood lead levels 32.3% (95% CI, 17.0 to 49.5) higher than those in the highest stratum.
Children living in the northeast sector had blood lead levels 10.9% (95% CI, 2.4 to 18.6) higher than those in the southwest.
The difference in lifetime blood lead between subcohorts born in 1987/1988 versus 1991/1992 was 43.0% (t = 5.919, df = 725.9, p < 0.0005).
There was a significant decrease (p < 0.01) in the percentage of children with blood lead ≥ 10 µg/dL across year of birth during the first 7 years of life.
captured_features: complete versus incomplete blood lead data
pathologies_diseases: lead exposure / elevated blood lead (≥10 µg/dL)
study_design: prospective birth cohort with repeated measures
population: 321 children born in Mexico City between 1987 and 1992, followed from birth through 10 years of age
limitations: Only three air monitoring stations were used to estimate annual atmospheric lead, which were not necessarily representative of each child's place of residence.
Use of lead-glazed ceramic pottery was not quantified and was assessed only at the start of the study using maternal self-report during pregnancy.
Air lead nested within subcohort showed collinearity with age of the child.
Address change was unverifiable for 53 subjects (16.5%), and data on these subjects are likely incomplete.
